commonMistakes: Sending a welcome for every new app instead of once per maker.
Running the flow under a personal admin account.
Writing an email longer than a screen.
Not enabling pagination, so busy environments are only partly read.
troubleshooting: If makers are welcomed twice, the lookup on the Makers list is failing. Check the email comparison and casing.
If the flow sees only one environment, the connection lacks a tenant admin role.
If creator details are empty for flows, resolve the creator's object ID with Office 365 Users.
If the run is slow, limit processing to environments that had changes or raise concurrency.
seoTitle: Welcome new makers automatically with an admin flow
seoDescription: A scheduled flow that finds people who created their first app or flow, sends them the rules and resources, and records them in a makers list.
primaryKeyword: Power Platform new maker welcome email

faqs.question: How do I find new Power Platform makers?
faqs.answer: List apps and flows as an admin, filter by creation date and compare the creators with a list of makers you have already recorded.

faqs.question: Does the CoE Starter Kit do this?
faqs.answer: Yes, it includes a welcome email process. This flow is a lighter option when the kit is not installed.

faqs.question: Which connectors list all apps and flows?
faqs.answer: Power Apps for Admins, Power Automate Management and Power Platform for Admins, run by an account with an admin role.

title: Export and audit DLP policies with PowerShell
shortDescription: List every data policy, the environments it covers and each connector's classification into a CSV, and check which policies apply to a given environment.
fullDescription: DLP policies stack: an environment can be covered by several, and the most restrictive result wins. The admin center shows one policy at a time, which makes it hard to answer what is actually allowed in an environment. A script that exports every policy with its scope and connector groups gives a single view to review and keep as evidence.
problemStatement: A maker asks why a connector is blocked in one environment but not another, and working it out means opening five policies in turn.
whenToUse: Quarterly governance reviews and audits
Troubleshooting why a connector is blocked
Keeping a history of policy changes
whenNotToUse: Editing policies in bulk by script without a tested rollback copy
Sharing the export widely, since it describes your controls
formulaOrCode:
# Requires: Install-Module Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell
Add-PowerAppsAccount

# 1. Policies and their scope
$policies = (Get-DlpPolicy).value
$scope = foreach ($p in $policies) {
    [pscustomobject]@{
        Policy       = $p.displayName
        PolicyId     = $p.name
        Scope        = $p.environmentType          # AllEnvironments | OnlyEnvironments | ExceptEnvironments
        Environments = ($p.environments.name -join "; ")
        Created      = $p.createdTime
        Modified     = $p.lastModifiedTime
        ModifiedBy   = $p.lastModifiedBy.displayName
    }
}
$scope | Export-Csv .\dlp-policies.csv -NoTypeInformation

# 2. Connector classification per policy
$rows = foreach ($p in $policies) {
    foreach ($g in $p.connectorGroups) {           # classification: Confidential (Business) | General (Non-business) | Blocked
        foreach ($c in $g.connectors) {
            [pscustomobject]@{
                Policy     = $p.displayName
                Group      = switch ($g.classification) { "Confidential" {"Business"} "General" {"Non-business"} default {$g.classification} }
                Connector  = $c.name
                ConnectorId= $c.id
            }
        }
    }
    [pscustomobject]@{ Policy = $p.displayName; Group = "(default for new connectors)"; Connector = $p.defaultConnectorsClassification; ConnectorId = "" }
}
$rows | Export-Csv .\dlp-connectors.csv -NoTypeInformation

# 3. Which policies apply to one environment
$envId = "<environment id>"
$applies = $policies | Where-Object {
    $_.environmentType -eq "AllEnvironments" -or
    ($_.environmentType -eq "OnlyEnvironments"   -and $_.environments.name -contains $envId) -or
    ($_.environmentType -eq "ExceptEnvironments" -and $_.environments.name -notcontains $envId)
}
$applies | Select-Object displayName, environmentType

# 4. Effective result for one connector in that environment
$connector = "shared_sql"
foreach ($p in $applies) {
    $g = $p.connectorGroups | Where-Object { $_.connectors.id -like "*/$connector" }
    "{0}: {1}" -f $p.displayName, ($(if ($g) { $g.classification } else { $p.defaultConnectorsClassification }))
}
# Blocked in any policy = blocked. Otherwise two connectors can be used together only if every policy puts
# them in the same group.

# 5. Keep a dated backup of full policy definitions
$stamp = Get-Date -Format "yyyyMMdd"
$policies | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Out-File ".\dlp-backup-$stamp.json"

# 6. Custom connector URL patterns and endpoint/action rules
Get-PowerAppDlpPolicyConnectorConfigurations -TenantId <tenant id> -PolicyName <policy id>
Get-PowerAppPolicyUrlPatterns -TenantId <tenant id> -PolicyName <policy id>

Review points
  Any policy with defaultConnectorsClassification = General while Business holds your data connectors is fine.
  A default of Confidential means every new connector joins your business data group automatically.
  Environments covered by no policy: compare the environment list with every policy's scope.
  HTTP, HTTP with Microsoft Entra ID and custom connectors: confirm where they are allowed and why.

Schedule
  Run monthly from an automation account or pipeline with a service principal, commit the CSV and JSON to a
  private repository, and review the diff.
stepByStepInstructions: Install the admin PowerShell module and sign in as a Power Platform administrator.
Export each policy's scope and environments.
Export connector classifications for every policy.
Work out which policies apply to each important environment.
Save a dated JSON backup of all policy definitions.
Review the output for unprotected environments and risky defaults.
commonMistakes: Reviewing policies one by one in the portal and missing overlaps.
Forgetting the default group for new connectors.
Assuming the least restrictive policy wins.
No backup before changing a policy.
troubleshooting: If Get-DlpPolicy returns nothing, the account lacks a tenant admin role.
If an environment appears unprotected, check for a tenant-wide policy with exceptions.
If the connector name is unclear, match on the id, which ends with the connector's internal name.
If a change broke flows, restore the previous definition from the dated JSON with Set-DlpPolicy.
seoTitle: Export and audit DLP policies with PowerShell
seoDescription: List every data policy, the environments it covers and each connector's classification into a CSV, and check which policies apply to a given environment.
primaryKeyword: Power Platform DLP policy PowerShell export

faqs.question: How do I list all DLP policies in Power Platform?
faqs.answer: Run Get-DlpPolicy from the Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell module as a tenant admin.

faqs.question: What happens when several DLP policies cover one environment?
faqs.answer: All of them apply. A connector blocked in any policy is blocked, and connectors must share a group in every policy to be used together.

faqs.question: Can I back up DLP policies?
faqs.answer: Yes. Export the policy objects to JSON on a schedule and keep them in a private repository.

title: Allow a connector but restrict its endpoints and actions
shortDescription: Go beyond block or allow: permit HTTP, SQL Server or custom connectors only for approved URLs and servers, and switch off individual connector actions.
fullDescription: Blocking the HTTP connector stops legitimate integrations. Allowing it opens every address on the internet. DLP policies have finer controls: endpoint filtering limits a connector to listed hosts, connector action control disables specific actions and triggers, and custom connector URL patterns classify custom connectors by their base address.
problemStatement: A project needs the HTTP connector for one internal API, so it is moved to Business for the whole environment, and now any flow can post data to any URL.
whenToUse: Allowing HTTP, SQL Server, Dataverse or Azure Blob for specific targets only
Disabling risky actions such as delete or send-as while keeping the connector
Governing custom connectors by host name
whenNotToUse: Long allow-lists maintained by hand with no owner
Treating endpoint filtering as a network firewall. It applies to Power Platform connectors only
formulaOrCode:
Where
  Power Platform admin center > Security > Data and privacy > Data policies > open a policy > Connectors
  Select a connector > ... > Configure connector
    Connector actions        Connector endpoints

1. Endpoint filtering
   Supported on HTTP, HTTP with Microsoft Entra ID, HTTP Webhook, SQL Server, Azure Blob Storage, SMTP,
   Browser Automation and UI Automation. Dataverse rules use the organisation ID, and the current
   environment is always allowed. Microsoft labels endpoint filtering as a preview feature.
   Rules apply to endpoints fixed at design time, not to values built at run time.
   Rules are evaluated top to bottom. First match wins. The last rule is the default.

   HTTP example
     Order  Endpoint                              Action
     1      https://api.contoso.com/*             Allow
     2      https://contoso.azure-api.net/*       Allow
     3      https://*.logic.azure.com/*           Allow       (only if child Logic Apps are approved)
     4      *                                     Deny
   SQL Server example (format: server,database)
     1      contoso-sql.database.windows.net,RequestHub      Allow
     2      contoso-sql.database.windows.net,*               Allow
     3      *                                                Deny
   Azure Blob example:  https://contosoprod.blob.core.windows.net/*   Allow, then * Deny
   Dataverse example:   https://contoso.crm.dynamics.com   Allow, then * Deny   (stops connecting to other orgs)

   Behaviour: flows calling a denied endpoint fail at run time, or at save when the value is static.
   Dynamic values (a URL built from a variable) are evaluated at run time.

2. Connector action control
   Configure connector > Connector actions: a toggle per action and trigger, plus
   "Default connector action settings": Allow or Deny for actions added to the connector later.
   Examples
     Office 365 Outlook      Deny: Send an email from a shared mailbox (V2) if send-as must be controlled
     SharePoint              Deny: Send an HTTP request to SharePoint, where REST calls are not permitted
     Microsoft Teams         Deny: Post as flow bot to a user where notifications are centralised
     Dataverse               Deny: Perform an unbound action in maker environments
   Set the default to Deny for high-risk connectors so new actions need a review.
   Works for connectors classified Business or Non-business. Blocked connectors need no action control.

3. Custom connector URL patterns
   Data policies > open policy > Custom connectors
     Order  Pattern                               Group
     1      https://api.contoso.com*              Business
     2      https://*.contoso.com*                Business
     3      https://partner.fabrikam.com/api*     Non-business
     4      *                                     Blocked
   A custom connector is classified by matching its host URL. The final * rule sets the default.

PowerShell (keep policies as code)
  Get-PowerAppDlpPolicyConnectorConfigurations -TenantId $tenant -PolicyName $policyId
  New-PowerAppDlpPolicyConnectorConfigurations -TenantId $tenant -PolicyName $policyId -NewDlpPolicyConnectorConfigurations $config
  $config.connectorActionConfigurations: connectorId, defaultConnectorActionRuleBehavior, actionRules[{actionId, behavior}]
  $config.endpointConfigurations:        connectorId, endpointRules[{order, endpoint, behavior}]
  Get-PowerAppPolicyUrlPatterns / New-PowerAppPolicyUrlPatterns for custom connector patterns.

Request process
  Makers request a new endpoint with: URL, owner of the target system, data classification, environment.
  Approver adds the narrowest pattern that works. Review the list every six months and remove unused entries.

Test
  In a sandbox covered by the policy: a flow calling an allowed URL succeeds. A call to https://example.org
  fails with a message that the endpoint is blocked by the data policy.
stepByStepInstructions: Identify connectors that are needed but too open, starting with HTTP and custom connectors.
Add endpoint rules allowing the approved hosts and denying everything else.
Disable connector actions that are not permitted and set the default for new actions.
Add custom connector URL patterns ending in a blocked default.
Test allowed and denied calls in a sandbox covered by the policy.
Set up a request and review process for new endpoints.
commonMistakes: Moving HTTP to Business with no endpoint rules.
Putting the deny-all rule above the allow rules.
Forgetting dynamic URLs are checked only at run time.
Allow-lists nobody owns or reviews.
troubleshooting: If an approved call is denied, check rule order and the exact host, including scheme and trailing path.
If a flow saves but fails when run, its URL is dynamic and resolves to a denied endpoint.
If a custom connector is blocked, its host matches no pattern above the default.
If an action still appears in the designer, the policy change may take time to apply. Save again after an hour.
seoTitle: Allow a connector but restrict its endpoints and actions
seoDescription: Go beyond block or allow: permit HTTP, SQL Server or custom connectors only for approved URLs and servers, and switch off individual connector actions.
primaryKeyword: Power Platform DLP endpoint filtering connector action control

faqs.question: Can I allow the HTTP connector for only some URLs?
faqs.answer: Yes. Endpoint filtering in a DLP policy lets you list allowed URL patterns and deny everything else.

faqs.question: Can I block one action of a connector?
faqs.answer: Yes. Connector action control in a DLP policy turns individual actions and triggers on or off.

faqs.question: How are custom connectors classified in DLP?
faqs.answer: By URL patterns matched against the connector's host, with a final rule that sets the default group.

title: Search Power Platform activity in the Microsoft Purview audit log
shortDescription: Find who created, edited, shared or deleted an app, flow, connection or DLP policy using the unified audit log, in the portal and with PowerShell.
fullDescription: Maker and admin activity across Power Apps, Power Automate, connectors and data policies is written to the Microsoft 365 unified audit log. It answers questions the admin center cannot: who shared an app with Everyone, who deleted a flow, who changed a DLP policy and when. Dataverse row-level auditing is separate and lives inside each environment.
problemStatement: A production flow has been deleted and a DLP policy changed. The admin center shows the current state but not who did it or when.
whenToUse: Investigating a change or deletion
Evidence for audits and security reviews
Alerting on sensitive actions such as sharing with Everyone
whenNotToUse: Looking for changes to Dataverse rows, which are in Dataverse auditing instead
Expecting events older than your licence's retention period
formulaOrCode:
Portal
  Microsoft Purview portal > Audit > New search
    Date and time range: start and end (UTC)
    Activities - friendly names: type "PowerApp", "flow" or "DLP" and select
    Record types: PowerAppsApp, PowerAppsPlan, MicrosoftFlow, PowerPlatformAdminDlp,
                  PowerPlatformAdminEnvironment, PowerAppsResource, PowerPlatformAdministratorActivity
    Users: optional          File, folder or site: leave empty
  Search runs as a job. Open it for results. Export > Download all results (CSV with an AuditData JSON column).

Operations worth knowing
  Power Apps      CreatePowerApp, UpdatePowerApp, PublishPowerApp, DeletePowerApp, LaunchPowerApp,
                  PowerAppPermissionEdited (sharing changes), DeletePowerAppPermission, RestorePowerApp
  Power Automate  CreateFlow, EditFlow, DeleteFlow, PutPermissions (sharing), DeletePermissions,
                  StartAPaidTrial, plus run-only user changes
  Connections     CreateConnection, DeleteConnection (PowerAppsResource / connector events)
  DLP             CreateDlpPolicy, UpdateDlpPolicy, DeleteDlpPolicy
  Environments    environment create, delete, copy, restore, property and lifecycle changes
  Admin           tenant setting changes, Managed Environments settings, role elevation

PowerShell (Exchange Online module)
  Install-Module ExchangeOnlineManagement
  Connect-ExchangeOnline
  $start = (Get-Date).AddDays(-7); $end = Get-Date

  # Who deleted flows in the last week
  Search-UnifiedAuditLog -StartDate $start -EndDate $end -RecordType MicrosoftFlow -Operations DeleteFlow -ResultSize 5000 |
    ForEach-Object { $d = $_.AuditData | ConvertFrom-Json
      [pscustomobject]@{ When = $_.CreationDate; Who = $_.UserIds; Operation = $_.Operations;
                         Flow = $d.FlowDetailsUrl; Environment = $d.EnvironmentName } }

  # App sharing changes, flagging tenant-wide shares
  Search-UnifiedAuditLog -StartDate $start -EndDate $end -RecordType PowerAppsApp -Operations PowerAppPermissionEdited -ResultSize 5000 |
    ForEach-Object { $d = $_.AuditData | ConvertFrom-Json
      [pscustomobject]@{ When = $_.CreationDate; Who = $_.UserIds; App = $d.AppName;
                         Target = ($d.AdditionalInfo | Out-String) } } |
    Where-Object { $_.Target -match "Tenant|Everyone" }

  # DLP policy changes
  Search-UnifiedAuditLog -StartDate $start -EndDate $end -RecordType PowerPlatformAdminDlp -ResultSize 1000 |
    Select-Object CreationDate, UserIds, Operations, AuditData

  More than 5000 results: page with -SessionId "pp" -SessionCommand ReturnLargeSet, repeating until empty.

Requirements
  Auditing is on by default for Microsoft 365 organisations. Check: Get-AdminAuditLogConfig | fl UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled
  Permissions: Audit Logs or View-Only Audit Logs role (Purview role groups: Audit Reader, Audit Manager).
  Retention: 180 days as standard. One year or longer with Audit (Premium) licences and retention policies.
  Events appear within about 60 to 90 minutes, sometimes longer.

Alerting
  Purview > Audit > search, then create an alert policy on the activity (Microsoft Defender portal >
  Policies > Alert policy > activity "PowerAppPermissionEdited"), or forward audit data to Microsoft Sentinel
  with the Microsoft 365 / Power Platform connectors and write analytic rules.
  Scheduled flow alternative: Office 365 Management Activity API (Audit.General content type) through an app
  registration, filtered to the operations above, posting to a Teams channel.

Dataverse activity
  Row create, update, delete and read auditing is configured per environment and table, and viewed in the
  environment's audit summary. With "Read logs" auditing enabled, user access events also flow to Purview
  under the Dynamics 365 / CRM record type.

Keep evidence
  Export results for an investigation promptly and store them with the incident record, since standard
  retention is limited.
stepByStepInstructions: Confirm unified audit logging is enabled and you hold an audit reader role.
Search by record type and operation for the time range in question.
Open or export results and read the AuditData details.
Use PowerShell for repeatable searches and larger result sets.
Create alerts for sensitive operations such as tenant-wide sharing or policy changes.
Export and file results for investigations before retention expires.
commonMistakes: Searching the Purview log for Dataverse row changes.
Searching in local time when the log uses UTC.
Expecting events within minutes of the action.
Relying on 180-day retention for annual audit evidence.
troubleshooting: If a search returns nothing, widen the time range and remove the user filter.
If you cannot open Audit, ask for the Audit Reader role group in Purview.
If results stop at 5000, page with a session ID and ReturnLargeSet.
If you need older events, check whether Audit (Premium) retention policies exist for those record types.
seoTitle: Search Power Platform activity in the Microsoft Purview audit log
seoDescription: Find who created, edited, shared or deleted an app, flow, connection or DLP policy using the unified audit log, in the portal and with PowerShell.

faqs.question: Where are Power Apps and Power Automate activities logged?
faqs.answer: In the Microsoft 365 unified audit log, searchable in the Microsoft Purview portal and with Search-UnifiedAuditLog.

faqs.question: Can I see who deleted a flow?
faqs.answer: Yes. Search for the DeleteFlow operation in the audit log for the relevant dates.

faqs.question: How long are the logs kept?
faqs.answer: 180 days as standard, and longer with Audit (Premium) licensing and a retention policy.

title: Understand and monitor Power Platform request limits
shortDescription: What counts as a Power Platform request, the daily allowance per licence, how throttling shows up in flows and apps, and how to see who is close to the limit.
fullDescription: Every connector action, Dataverse call and flow action counts as a Power Platform request against the licence of the user or flow owner. Limits are generous for normal use, but high-volume flows under one service account reach them. Throttled flows slow down or fail with 429 responses. Knowing the allowances and how to read the usage reports avoids surprises.
problemStatement: A nightly flow that updates fifty thousand rows starts taking ten hours and showing retry warnings, and nobody knows whether it is a bug or a limit.
whenToUse: High-volume flows and integrations
Choosing which account or licence a flow should run under
Explaining slow or throttled flows
whenNotToUse: Splitting work across many user accounts just to dodge limits, which breaches licence terms
Treating published limits as guaranteed throughput
formulaOrCode:
Daily allowances (per 24 hours, per user or flow)
  Paid licensed users: Power Apps Premium, Power Automate Premium, Dynamics 365 (except Team Member)    40,000
  Microsoft 365 licences, Power Apps per app, Dynamics 365 Team Member                                   6,000
  Power Automate Process (per flow) licence                                                            250,000 per flow
  Non-licensed users: application users, service principals (pooled at tenant level)                  500,000 base
                                                                                                       plus accrual per licence
  Copilot Studio and others have their own allowances.
  A transition period currently applies with more generous enforcement. Reports show usage against the stated limits.

What counts
  Power Automate: every action run, including each iteration's actions inside Apply to each, plus trigger checks
  that fire. Scopes, conditions and variable actions count.
  Power Apps: each connector call and Dataverse request (Patch, Filter that goes to the server, and so on).
  Dataverse API: each request, including each operation inside a batch.

Whose allowance
  Automated and scheduled flows: the flow OWNER (primary owner). Instant flows: the user who runs them.
  Flows with a Process licence: the flow's own allowance.
  Flows owned by a service principal: the non-licensed tenant pool, or a Process licence.

Signs of throttling
  Flow run: actions show "retried" with status 429 and a Retry-After header. Run duration grows.
  Flow details: a banner "Your flow is being throttled" or performance profile messages.
  Dataverse service protection (separate, per user per 5 minutes): 6,000 requests, 20 minutes of execution time,
  52 concurrent requests. Error codes 0x80072322, 0x80072321, 0x80072326.
  Connector limits (separate again): for example SharePoint 600 calls per minute per connection.

See usage
  Power Platform admin center > Licensing > Capacity add-ons > Power Platform requests (or Reports):
    Licensed user report, Non-licensed user report, Per flow licensed flows report
    Download: per day and per user or flow, with entitled quantity and consumed quantity.
  Power Automate portal > flow > Analytics > Actions: actions per day for one flow.
  Estimate: actions per run x runs per day. A loop of 50,000 items with 3 actions inside = 150,000+ requests.

Reduce requests
  Filter at the source with OData filters and trigger conditions so fewer runs start.
  Replace Apply to each with Select and Filter array for data shaping.
  Batch writes: Dataverse changesets or SharePoint $batch send many operations in one action
  (Dataverse still counts each operation, connectors count one action).
  Avoid polling triggers with short intervals. Prefer event triggers.
  Move bulk data movement to dataflows or Azure Data Factory, which are not counted the same way.
  Spread scheduled loads across the day rather than one burst.

Increase the allowance
  Assign a Process licence to a high-volume flow.
  Buy Power Platform request capacity add-ons (assigned to users or flows in the admin center).
  Move ownership to a properly licensed service account with a Premium licence.

Handle 429 gracefully
  Leave the default retry policy on (exponential, honours Retry-After). For custom HTTP calls, set
  Retry Policy: Exponential, count 4 to 8, minimum interval PT10S.
  Lower Apply to each concurrency if parallel calls trigger connector limits.
stepByStepInstructions: Work out which licence and owner each high-volume flow runs under.
Estimate daily requests as actions per run multiplied by runs.
Download the request usage reports from the admin center.
Check throttled flows for 429 retries and long durations.
Redesign loops and triggers to cut actions.
Assign Process licences or add-on capacity where volume is justified.
commonMistakes: Counting runs instead of actions.
Running every high-volume flow under one user's allowance.
Confusing Dataverse service protection limits with daily request limits.
Removing the retry policy to make failures visible, which turns slow flows into failed ones.
troubleshooting: If a flow slows after growth in data, count its actions per run and compare with the owner's allowance.
If only Dataverse actions are throttled in bursts, reduce concurrency. That is service protection.
If only one connector is throttled, check that connector's own limits.
If the report shows a service principal over the pool, assign a Process licence to its flows.
seoTitle: Understand and monitor Power Platform request limits
seoDescription: What counts as a Power Platform request, the daily allowance per licence, how throttling shows up in flows and apps, and how to see who is close to the limit.

faqs.question: What is a Power Platform request?
faqs.answer: Any action a flow runs, or any connector or Dataverse call an app makes. Each counts toward a daily allowance tied to the licence.

faqs.question: Whose limit does a scheduled flow use?
faqs.answer: The flow owner's, unless the flow has its own Process licence.

faqs.question: What happens when the limit is reached?
faqs.answer: Flows are slowed with 429 responses and retries. Sustained overuse can lead to the flow being turned off after notification.

title: Reassign apps, flows and connections when a maker leaves
shortDescription: An offboarding routine: inventory what the leaver owns, add new owners to apps and flows, replace their connections and deal with Dataverse row ownership.
fullDescription: When a maker's account is disabled, their flows stop as soon as connection tokens expire, and their apps can no longer be edited. The fix is simple before they leave and awkward afterwards. A short routine run at notice time keeps everything working and leaves nothing ownerless.
problemStatement: A departed employee's flow fails three weeks after they left, because its SharePoint connection belonged to their now-disabled account, and nobody has rights to edit it.
whenToUse: Employee departures and role changes
Contractor engagements ending
Clearing existing orphaned apps and flows
whenNotToUse: Keeping the leaver's account enabled as a workaround
Reassigning everything to one administrator personally instead of a team or service account
formulaOrCode:
1. Inventory (PowerShell, as Power Platform admin)
  $upn = "leaver@contoso.com"
  $user = Get-UsersOrGroupsFromGraph -SearchString $upn | Select-Object -First 1      # ObjectId
  $id = $user.ObjectId
  $apps  = Get-AdminPowerApp -Owner $id
  $flows = Get-AdminFlow -CreatedBy $id
  $conns = Get-AdminPowerAppConnection -CreatedBy $id
  $apps  | Select-Object DisplayName, EnvironmentName, AppName, LastModifiedTime | Export-Csv apps.csv -NoTypeInformation
  $flows | Select-Object DisplayName, EnvironmentName, FlowName, Enabled | Export-Csv flows.csv -NoTypeInformation
  $conns | Select-Object DisplayName, ConnectorName, EnvironmentName | Export-Csv connections.csv -NoTypeInformation
  Also: flows where they are a co-owner, custom connectors they created, gateways they administer,
  Dataverse rows they own, and Power BI workspaces.

2. Decide per item with the leaver and their manager: Keep (new owner), Retire, or Personal (delete).

3. Canvas apps: set a new owner
  Set-AdminPowerAppOwner -AppName <app id> -EnvironmentName <env id> -AppOwner <new owner object id>
  The previous owner keeps view access to the app. Remove them afterwards:
  Remove-AdminPowerAppRoleAssignment -AppName <app id> -EnvironmentName <env id> -RoleId <role assignment id>
  Add a second co-owner or a security group as co-owner so the app never has a single owner again.

4. Cloud flows
  Non-solution flows: the creator cannot be changed. Add owners:
    Set-AdminFlowOwnerRole -EnvironmentName <env id> -FlowName <flow id> -PrincipalType User -PrincipalObjectId <new id> -RoleName CanEdit
  Solution flows: change the primary owner
    Flow details > Edit > Owner, or  PATCH /api/data/v9.2/workflows(<id>) { "ownerid@odata.bind": "/systemusers(<new user id>)" }
  Then, as the new owner, open each flow and replace connections:
    Flow details > Connections (or connection references) > switch each to the new owner's or the service
    account's connection > Save > run a test.
  Licensing: premium flows need the NEW owner to hold the right licence.

5. Connections and connection references
  Connections cannot be transferred. Create new ones under the service account, then update each connection
  reference (solution > Connection references > Edit > pick the new connection).
  Delete the leaver's connections once nothing uses them:
    Remove-AdminPowerAppConnection -EnvironmentName <env id> -ConnectorName <name> -ConnectionName <id>

6. Dataverse rows
  Environment > Settings > Users > select the user > Reassign records > assign to another user or team.
  Bulk and silent. Check business rules that depend on owner.
  The user record is disabled automatically once the account is disabled or unlicensed.

7. Other items
  Custom connectors: Share with the new owner as "Can edit". In solutions, ownership follows the Dataverse row.
  On-premises data gateways: add another admin before the leaver goes (Power Platform admin center > Data > Gateways).
  Approvals in progress assigned to the leaver: reassign from the approvals centre or cancel and restart.
  Teams and SharePoint sites the flows use: confirm the new owner has access.
  Power BI: transfer dataset ownership (Take over) and workspace admin.

8. After the account is disabled
  Orphaned items can still be recovered by an admin with the same commands. Flows whose owner is missing appear
  in the admin center with no owner. Assign one and repair connections.

Prevent it
  Production flows and apps owned by a service account or team from the start, deployed through solutions.
  Add the routine to the HR leaver checklist with ten working days' notice.
stepByStepInstructions: List the apps, flows, connections and other resources the leaver owns.
Agree with their manager what to keep, retire or delete.
Assign new owners to apps and flows, preferably a service account plus a named backup.
Recreate connections under the new owner and update connection references.
Reassign Dataverse rows, gateways, connectors and in-progress approvals.
Test each kept flow and app, then remove the leaver's access.
commonMistakes: Waiting until the account is disabled.
Adding a new owner but leaving the leaver's connections in use.
Reassigning to a single admin who becomes the next single point of failure.
Forgetting gateways and custom connectors.
troubleshooting: If a flow fails after the handover, a connection still belongs to the leaver. Replace it.
If the new owner cannot turn on a premium flow, they need a suitable licence.
If an app cannot be edited, set a new owner as admin with Set-AdminPowerAppOwner.
If rows are still owned by the disabled user, run Reassign records from their user record.
seoTitle: Reassign apps, flows and connections when a maker leaves
seoDescription: An offboarding routine: inventory what the leaver owns, add new owners to apps and flows, replace their connections and deal with Dataverse row ownership.
primaryKeyword: reassign Power Apps flows owner leaves

faqs.question: What happens to flows when the owner leaves?
faqs.answer: They keep running until the owner's connections stop authenticating, then fail. Without another owner, nobody can repair them except an admin.

faqs.question: Can I change the owner of a Power Apps canvas app?
faqs.answer: Yes. An admin can run Set-AdminPowerAppOwner to assign a new owner.

faqs.question: Can connections be transferred to another user?
faqs.answer: No. Create new connections under the new owner and switch flows and connection references to them.

title: Quarantine a risky canvas app without deleting it
shortDescription: Block users from opening a canvas app while its owner fixes a compliance problem, using admin PowerShell, and release it when resolved.
fullDescription: Sometimes an app has to be stopped immediately: it exposes data too widely, uses a connector that is about to be blocked, or has no owner. Deleting it destroys work. Quarantine keeps the app and its sharing in place but prevents users from launching it. Makers can still open it in Studio to fix the issue.
problemStatement: An app shared with the whole organisation shows salary data from a list with broken permissions. It must stop now, but the team needs it back once fixed.
whenToUse: Apps that breach policy and need urgent containment
Unowned apps awaiting a decision
A step in a compliance process before deletion
whenNotToUse: Routine nudges to makers, where an email is enough
Model-driven apps and flows, which need other controls
formulaOrCode:
# Requires the admin module and a Power Platform admin (or environment admin) sign-in
Install-Module Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell
Add-PowerAppsAccount

# Find the app
Get-AdminPowerApp "Salary Review" | Select-Object DisplayName, AppName, EnvironmentName, Owner
$envId = "<environment id>"
$appId = "<app id (AppName)>"

# Check current state
Get-AppQuarantineState -EnvironmentName $envId -AppName $appId
#   QuarantineStatus : Unquarantined

# Quarantine
Set-AppAsQuarantined -EnvironmentName $envId -AppName $appId

# Release when fixed
Set-AppAsUnquarantined -EnvironmentName $envId -AppName $appId

What users experience
  Launching the app (web, mobile, Teams) shows a message that the app has been quarantined by an administrator.
  Owners and co-owners can still open it in Power Apps Studio to edit, save and publish.
  Sharing, connections and data are untouched.

Containment checklist for a data exposure
  1. Quarantine the app (seconds).
  2. Fix the source: SharePoint list permissions, Dataverse roles or the app's filter. The app was only a window.
     If the data source itself is over-shared, users can still reach it directly.
  3. Turn off related flows if they send the data onwards.
  4. Tell the owner and the users, with a named contact.
  5. Review who opened the app: Purview audit log, operation LaunchPowerApp, for the exposure period.
  6. Release after review by a second person.

Other containment tools
  Remove broad sharing but keep the app available to its core team:
    Get-AdminPowerAppRoleAssignment -AppName $appId -EnvironmentName $envId
    Remove-AdminPowerAppRoleAssignment -AppName $appId -EnvironmentName $envId -RoleId <id of the Everyone/tenant share>
  Require conditional access for one app (Entra authentication context):
    Set-AdminPowerAppConditionalAccessAuthenticationContextIds -EnvironmentName $envId -AppName $appId -AuthenticationContextIds <id>
  Flows: Disable-AdminFlow -EnvironmentName $envId -FlowName <flow id>
  Delete, recoverable for a limited time:
    Remove-AdminPowerApp -AppName $appId -EnvironmentName $envId
    Get-AdminDeletedPowerAppsList -EnvironmentName $envId
    Get-AdminRecoverDeletedPowerApp -AppName $appId -EnvironmentName $envId

Bulk: quarantine apps whose owner has left
  Get-AdminPowerApp -EnvironmentName $envId | Where-Object { -not $_.Owner.displayName } |
    ForEach-Object { Set-AppAsQuarantined -EnvironmentName $envId -AppName $_.AppName }
  Announce first, and keep a list of what was quarantined and why.

Record
  Log each quarantine: app, environment, reason, who decided, date, release date. The CoE Starter Kit's
  compliance process can drive this with maker notifications.
stepByStepInstructions: Identify the app's ID and environment.
Quarantine it with Set-AppAsQuarantined.
Fix the underlying data access problem, not just the app.
Inform the owner and users with the reason and a contact.
Review audit logs for use during the exposure.
Release the app after a second person confirms the fix.
commonMistakes: Deleting the app and losing the work.
Quarantining the app but leaving the over-shared data source open.
No communication, so users raise support tickets.
Forgetting to release or follow up.
troubleshooting: If users can still open the app, confirm the state with Get-AppQuarantineState and that you targeted the right environment.
If the cmdlets are missing, update the administration module.
If the owner cannot edit the app, check they are still an owner. Quarantine does not remove edit access.
If the data is still exposed, fix permissions at the source.
seoTitle: Quarantine a risky canvas app without deleting it
seoDescription: Block users from opening a canvas app while its owner fixes a compliance problem, using admin PowerShell, and release it when resolved.

faqs.question: How do I disable a Power Apps canvas app without deleting it?
faqs.answer: Run Set-AppAsQuarantined as an admin. Users cannot launch it, but owners can still edit it.

faqs.question: Does quarantine remove sharing?
faqs.answer: No. Sharing and connections stay as they are and apply again when the app is released.

faqs.question: Can deleted canvas apps be recovered?
faqs.answer: For a limited time, with Get-AdminDeletedPowerAppsList and Get-AdminRecoverDeletedPowerApp.

title: Provision environments from an approved request
shortDescription: A request list, an approval and a flow that creates the environment with the right type, region, security group and DLP policy, then records it.
fullDescription: Restricting environment creation to admins prevents sprawl but creates a queue. A request process removes the bottleneck: makers fill in a short form, an approver checks capacity and purpose, and a flow creates the environment with standard settings. Every environment then has an owner, a purpose and an expiry on record.
problemStatement: Environment creation is locked down, so requests arrive by chat and email. Each is built by hand with different settings, and nobody tracks why an environment exists.
whenToUse: Tenants that restrict environment creation to admins
Standardising naming, security groups and policies
Tracking owners, purpose and review dates
whenNotToUse: Tiny tenants where an admin creates two environments a year
Skipping the capacity check and approving everything automatically
formulaOrCode:
Request list: Environment Requests (SharePoint or Dataverse)
  Title (project name), Purpose (multi-line), EnvType (Sandbox | Production | Developer),
  Region (choice), NeedsDataverse (yes/no), Language, Currency, Owner (person), BackupOwner (person),
  DataClassification (Public | Internal | Confidential), ExpectedUsers (number), ReviewDate (date),
  Status (Submitted | Approved | Rejected | Provisioning | Ready | Failed), EnvironmentId, EnvironmentUrl

Naming standard
  <Dept>-<Project>-<Stage>      for example  FIN-RequestHub-Test        URL: contoso-fin-requesthub-test

Flow: Provision environment
  Trigger: SharePoint > When an item is created (Environment Requests)
  1. Capacity check
       Power Platform for Admins > List Environments as Admin > count, or read a capacity figure kept in a
       settings list. If NeedsDataverse and free database capacity is under 1 GB: set Status Rejected with the
       reason and stop.
  2. Approval: Start and wait for an approval (platform team). Details: purpose, type, owner, classification.
       Rejected: update Status, email the requester with comments, Terminate.
  3. Security group
       Office 365 Groups / Microsoft Entra ID > Create group: "PP-<Title>-<Stage>-Users" (security)
       Add Owner and BackupOwner as members.
  4. Create the environment
       Power Platform for Admins > Create Environment
         Location: Region        Display name: per naming standard        Environment SKU: EnvType
       Then, if NeedsDataverse:
       Power Platform for Admins > Create Database (Create CDS Database)
         Environment: id from the previous step        Base language: 1033        Currency: USD
         (security group can be set through the environment's properties after creation)
     PowerShell or CLI alternative inside an Azure Automation runbook:
       pac admin create --name "FIN-RequestHub-Test" --type Sandbox --region unitedstates --currency USD
           --language 1033 --domain contoso-fin-requesthub-test --security-group-id <group id>
  5. Wait until ready
       Do until: Get Environment as Admin > properties/provisioningState equals Succeeded  (delay 1 minute, limit 30)
  6. Apply policy
       Add the environment to the right DLP policy by classification:
       Power Platform for Admins > Get DLP Policy V2 > append the environment > Update DLP Policy V2
       Optionally enable Managed Environments and add to an environment group so rules apply automatically.
  7. Grant the owner access
       Force Sync user, then assign System Administrator (Sandbox) or Environment Maker (per your standard)
       through the Dataverse connector: Relate rows systemuser <> role, or add them to a group team.
  8. Record and notify
       Update the request: Status Ready, EnvironmentId, EnvironmentUrl
       Email owner and backup: URL, rules for the environment, review date, how to request changes.
  Error path: Scope with run-after on failure > Status Failed, post details to the platform team channel.

Lifecycle
  Scheduled flow monthly: requests where ReviewDate is within 30 days > ask the owner to confirm the
  environment is still needed. No reply after two reminders: escalate to the backup owner, then schedule
  deletion with notice. Sandboxes for projects default to a 12-month review date.

Tenant settings to pair with this
  Production and Trial environment assignments: only specific admins. Developer: everyone (with routing).

Without building it yourself
  The CoE Starter Kit includes an environment request management process with similar steps.
stepByStepInstructions: Restrict production and trial environment creation to admins in tenant settings.
Create a request list capturing purpose, type, owner, classification and review date.
Build a flow that checks capacity and asks the platform team to approve.
Create the security group and environment with standard naming and settings.
Add the environment to the right DLP policy and grant the owner access.
Record the result and schedule periodic reviews of each environment.
commonMistakes: Creating environments with no recorded owner or purpose.
Skipping the security group, leaving the environment open to all licensed users.
Forgetting to add the new environment to a DLP policy.
No review date, so project sandboxes live forever.
troubleshooting: If creation fails, check capacity, that the domain name is unique and that the region supports the type.
If the database step times out, poll the provisioning state for longer before continuing.
If the owner cannot sign in, they are not in the security group or have not been synced.
If the environment has no policy, check the DLP update step and tenant-wide policy scope.
seoTitle: Provision environments from an approved request
seoDescription: A request list, an approval and a flow that creates the environment with the right type, region, security group and DLP policy, then records it.

faqs.question: How do I control who can create Power Platform environments?
faqs.answer: Tenant settings in the admin center can limit production, sandbox and trial environment creation to specific admins.

faqs.question: Can a flow create an environment?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Power Platform for Admins connector has actions to create an environment and its Dataverse database.

faqs.question: What should an environment request capture?
faqs.answer: Purpose, type, region, owner and backup owner, data classification, expected users and a review date.

title: Collect form data in Teams with an Adaptive Card
shortDescription: Build a card with text, date, choice and toggle inputs, mark fields as required, post it from a flow and read each answer by its input ID.
fullDescription: An Adaptive Card can be a small form inside a Teams chat or channel. Each input has an ID. When the user presses a submit button, the flow receives a data object keyed by those IDs. Required fields and error messages are handled by the card, so the flow only receives complete answers.
problemStatement: A flow needs three facts from a manager before it can continue. Sending an email and parsing the reply is fragile, and a full app is too much for three fields.
whenToUse: Short structured questions inside a flow
Collecting a reason, date or choice from one person
Replacing reply-by-email steps
whenNotToUse: Long forms with many fields, where an app or Microsoft Forms is easier to use
Inputs that need lookups against large data sets
formulaOrCode:
Flow action
  Microsoft Teams > Post adaptive card and wait for a response
    Post as: Flow bot        Post in: Chat with Flow bot        Recipient: manager's email
    Update message: "Thanks, your answer was recorded."
    Message (the card JSON):

{
  "type": "AdaptiveCard",
  "$schema": "http://adaptivecards.io/schemas/adaptive-card.json",
  "version": "1.4",
  "body": [
    { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "Extension request: @{triggerOutputs()?['body/Title']}", "weight": "Bolder", "size": "Medium", "wrap": true },
    { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "Requested by @{triggerOutputs()?['body/Author/DisplayName']}", "isSubtle": true, "wrap": true },
    { "type": "Input.ChoiceSet", "id": "decision", "label": "Decision", "isRequired": true,
      "errorMessage": "Choose a decision", "style": "expanded",
      "choices": [ { "title": "Approve", "value": "Approved" }, { "title": "Decline", "value": "Declined" } ] },
    { "type": "Input.Date", "id": "newDueDate", "label": "New due date",
      "min": "@{formatDateTime(utcNow(),'yyyy-MM-dd')}", "errorMessage": "Pick a date from today onwards" },
    { "type": "Input.Number", "id": "extraBudget", "label": "Extra budget (USD)", "min": 0, "max": 50000, "value": 0 },
    { "type": "Input.Text", "id": "comments", "label": "Comments", "isMultiline": true, "maxLength": 500,
      "isRequired": true, "errorMessage": "A comment is required" },
    { "type": "Input.Toggle", "id": "notifyTeam", "title": "Notify the project team", "value": "true",
      "valueOn": "true", "valueOff": "false" }
  ],
  "actions": [
    { "type": "Action.Submit", "title": "Send", "data": { "action": "send" } },
    { "type": "Action.Submit", "title": "Ask me later", "data": { "action": "later" }, "associatedInputs": "none" }
  ]
}

Read the answers (dynamic content, or expressions)
  body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['decision']        Approved | Declined
  body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['newDueDate']      2026-12-04
  body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['extraBudget']     number as text
  body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['comments']
  body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['notifyTeam']      "true" | "false" (text)
  body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['action']          send | later
  body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['responder']?['email']      who answered

Convert types
  Number:  float(coalesce(body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['extraBudget'], '0'))
  Toggle:  equals(body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['notifyTeam'], 'true')
  Date:    empty when not filled. Guard with coalesce or a condition.

Notes on validation
  isRequired and errorMessage need a label on the input and card version 1.3 or later.
  "associatedInputs": "none" lets a button submit without validating or sending the inputs.
  Input.Text also supports "regex": "^[A-Z]{3}-\\d{4}$" with an errorMessage for format checks, and
  "style": "Email" | "Tel" | "Url" for the right mobile keyboard.

Timeout
  Action settings > Timeout: P2D. Add a parallel branch or a following action with run after "has timed out"
  to remind or escalate.

Design the card
  Adaptive Cards Designer (adaptivecards.io/designer or the Teams Developer Portal). Host app: Microsoft Teams.
  Build with sample data, then paste the JSON into the flow and replace values with dynamic content.
stepByStepInstructions: Design the card in the Adaptive Cards Designer with Teams as the host app.
Give every input a clear ID and a label.
Mark required inputs and add error messages.
Paste the JSON into Post adaptive card and wait for a response.
Read each value from the response data by input ID and convert types.
Set a timeout and handle the no-answer path.
commonMistakes: Inputs without IDs, so nothing comes back.
Using hint text inside the box as the only label.
Treating toggle and number values as typed values when they arrive as text.
No timeout, leaving the flow waiting for 30 days.
troubleshooting: If the card fails to post, validate the JSON and check the version is supported by Teams (1.4 is safe, 1.5 for most features).
If required validation does not fire, add a label and check the card version.
If a value is empty in the flow, compare the input ID with the expression's property name.
If the dynamic content list shows no inputs, save the flow once after pasting the card.
seoTitle: Collect form data in Teams with an Adaptive Card
seoDescription: Build a card with text, date, choice and toggle inputs, mark fields as required, post it from a flow and read each answer by its input ID.
primaryKeyword: Adaptive Card input form Teams Power Automate

faqs.question: How do I get user input from an Adaptive Card in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Use Post adaptive card and wait for a response. Each input's value is returned in the data object under the input's ID.

faqs.question: Can Adaptive Card inputs be required?
faqs.answer: Yes. Set isRequired with a label and an errorMessage on the input, using card version 1.3 or later.

faqs.question: Which Adaptive Card version does Teams support?
faqs.answer: Version 1.4 works everywhere in Teams, and 1.5 features are supported in most clients.

title: Update a Teams Adaptive Card after someone acts on it
shortDescription: Replace a posted card with a new version showing the outcome, so a channel does not keep displaying live buttons for a request that is already handled.
fullDescription: A card posted to a channel stays as it was unless the flow changes it. After the first person responds, the others still see buttons. Updating the card in place with the result, who acted and when, keeps the channel accurate and stops duplicate decisions.
problemStatement: A request card is posted to a team channel. One person approves it, but the card still shows Approve and Reject to everyone else an hour later.
whenToUse: Cards posted to channels or group chats where several people can act
Showing the final status on the original message
Long-running requests whose status changes
whenNotToUse: One-to-one cards where the built-in update message is enough
Updating cards posted by a different identity, which fails
formulaOrCode:
Option 1: built-in update on the waiting action
  Post adaptive card and wait for a response
    Update message: Decision recorded.
    Should update card: Yes
  After a response, the card is replaced by the update message text. Simple, but only text.

Option 2: replace with a full result card
  1. Post adaptive card and wait for a response
       Post as: Flow bot      Post in: Channel      Team / Channel: Requests
       (the action returns the message ID after the response)
  2. Update an adaptive card in a chat or channel
       Post as: Flow bot      Post in: Channel      Team / Channel: same as step 1
       Message ID: body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['messageId']
       Adaptive Card:
{
  "type": "AdaptiveCard", "$schema": "http://adaptivecards.io/schemas/adaptive-card.json", "version": "1.4",
  "body": [
    { "type": "ColumnSet", "columns": [
      { "type": "Column", "width": "stretch", "items": [
        { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "@{triggerOutputs()?['body/Title']}", "weight": "Bolder", "wrap": true } ] },
      { "type": "Column", "width": "auto", "items": [
        { "type": "TextBlock",
          "text": "@{body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['decision']}",
          "color": "@{if(equals(body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['decision'],'Approved'),'Good','Attention')}",
          "weight": "Bolder" } ] } ] },
    { "type": "FactSet", "facts": [
      { "title": "Decided by", "value": "@{body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['responder']?['displayName']}" },
      { "title": "When", "value": "@{convertFromUtc(utcNow(),'Eastern Standard Time','dd MMM yyyy HH:mm')}" },
      { "title": "Comment", "value": "@{body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['comments']}" } ] }
  ],
  "actions": [ { "type": "Action.OpenUrl", "title": "Open request", "url": "@{triggerOutputs()?['body/{Link}']}" } ]
}

Option 3: post now, update later from another flow
  Flow A: Post card in a chat or channel (the non-waiting action) > returns  outputs('Post_card')?['body/id']
          Save it on the record: Update item > TeamsMessageId = that id (and the team and channel IDs).
  Flow B (status changes days later): Update an adaptive card in a chat or channel with the stored Message ID.
  The card in Flow A should use Action.OpenUrl buttons only, since nothing is waiting for Action.Submit.

Rules
  The same identity that posted the card must update it: Flow bot updates Flow bot cards, a user updates
  their own. Post in and the team, channel or chat must match the original.
  Group chat: keep the chat ID as well as the message ID.
  Deleted messages cannot be updated: the action fails with NotFound. Handle with run after.

First responder wins
  Post adaptive card and wait for a response continues on the first submission. Updating the card straight
  afterwards removes the buttons for everyone else. If two people submit within the same second, the second
  sees an error that the card is no longer active.
stepByStepInstructions: Post the card with the waiting action in the channel.
Capture the message ID from the action's output.
Build a result card showing decision, responder, time and comment.
Call Update an adaptive card in a chat or channel with the same location and message ID.
Store message, team and channel IDs on the record if later flows need to update the card.
Handle failure when the original message was deleted.
commonMistakes: Leaving live buttons on a card after a decision.
Updating with a different Post as identity than the one that posted.
Not saving the message ID for later updates.
Using Action.Submit on cards posted without a waiting action.
troubleshooting: If the update fails with forbidden or not found, check Post as, team, channel and message ID all match the original post.
If the message ID is empty, read it after the response from the waiting action's body.
If the card does not change visually, the JSON is identical or invalid. Test it in the designer.
If the update lands on the wrong card, the stored ID belongs to another item. Save it immediately after posting.
seoTitle: Update a Teams Adaptive Card after someone acts on it
seoDescription: Replace a posted card with a new version showing the outcome, so a channel does not keep displaying live buttons for a request that is already handled.
primaryKeyword: update adaptive card Teams Power Automate

faqs.question: Can a flow change a card it already posted in Teams?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use Update an adaptive card in a chat or channel with the original message ID and the same posting identity.

faqs.question: Where do I get the message ID?
faqs.answer: From the output of the action that posted the card. The waiting action returns it after a response.

faqs.question: Can a card be updated days later?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you stored the message ID and its team, channel or chat when it was posted.

title: Show and hide parts of an Adaptive Card
shortDescription: Keep cards short with expandable details, a reject button that reveals a reason box, and sections that only appear when the data calls for them.
fullDescription: Cards in a busy channel need to be compact. Action.ToggleVisibility expands and collapses elements on the client with no flow involved. Action.ShowCard reveals a nested card with its own inputs and submit button. Conditional isVisible values set from flow data hide sections that do not apply.
problemStatement: A request card shows fifteen lines of detail that most readers do not need, and the reject path needs a reason that approve does not.
whenToUse: Long details that only some readers need
Different inputs for different buttons
Sections that apply only to some records
whenNotToUse: Hiding information people must read before deciding
Deep nesting of ShowCards, which is awkward on mobile
formulaOrCode:
1. Expand and collapse details (no round trip)
{
  "type": "AdaptiveCard", "$schema": "http://adaptivecards.io/schemas/adaptive-card.json", "version": "1.4",
  "body": [
    { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "Purchase request PR-1042", "weight": "Bolder", "size": "Medium" },
    { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "Laptop replacement, USD 1,850, Finance", "wrap": true },
    { "type": "ActionSet", "actions": [
      { "type": "Action.ToggleVisibility", "title": "Show details",
        "targetElements": [ "detailsBlock" ] } ] },
    { "type": "Container", "id": "detailsBlock", "isVisible": false, "items": [
      { "type": "FactSet", "facts": [
        { "title": "Supplier", "value": "Contoso Hardware" },
        { "title": "Cost centre", "value": "FIN-200" },
        { "title": "Justification", "value": "Current device is out of warranty." } ] } ] }
  ]
}

   Swap the button label too: two elements, toggled together
      { "type": "Action.ToggleVisibility", "title": "Show details", "targetElements": [ "detailsBlock", "showBtn", "hideBtn" ] }
   Set explicit states instead of flipping:
      "targetElements": [ { "elementId": "detailsBlock", "isVisible": true }, { "elementId": "summary", "isVisible": false } ]

2. Reject needs a reason: Action.ShowCard
  "actions": [
    { "type": "Action.Submit", "title": "Approve", "style": "positive", "data": { "decision": "Approved" } },
    { "type": "Action.ShowCard", "title": "Reject", "card": {
        "type": "AdaptiveCard",
        "body": [
          { "type": "Input.Text", "id": "rejectReason", "label": "Reason for rejecting", "isMultiline": true,
            "isRequired": true, "errorMessage": "Give a reason" } ],
        "actions": [
          { "type": "Action.Submit", "title": "Confirm reject", "style": "destructive", "data": { "decision": "Rejected" } } ] } }
  ]
  In the flow:
    body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['decision']
    body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['rejectReason']
  The Approve button sits outside the ShowCard, so the required reason does not block it.

3. Sections that depend on the data (set by the flow)
    { "type": "Container", "isVisible": @{greater(triggerOutputs()?['body/Amount'], 5000)}, "style": "warning", "items": [
      { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "Over USD 5,000: finance director approval also required.", "wrap": true } ] }
  The expression writes true or false without quotes, which is valid JSON for a boolean.
  For optional text: "isVisible": @{not(empty(triggerOutputs()?['body/Notes']))}

4. Overflow menu for secondary actions
  { "type": "Action.OpenUrl", "title": "View history", "url": "https://...", "mode": "secondary" }
  Secondary actions appear under the ... menu (version 1.5).

Behaviour notes
  ToggleVisibility state is local to each viewer and resets when the card reloads.
  Hidden inputs are still submitted with their current values.
  Teams shows up to six primary actions. Extra ones may be dropped: use ShowCard or secondary mode.
  Test on desktop and mobile: ShowCard opens inline in Teams.
stepByStepInstructions: Decide which parts of the card are summary and which are detail.
Wrap details in a container with an ID and isVisible false.
Add an Action.ToggleVisibility targeting that ID.
Use Action.ShowCard for buttons that need extra input.
Set isVisible from flow expressions for data-dependent sections.
Test the card on desktop and mobile Teams.
commonMistakes: Putting the reject reason on the main card as required, which blocks approval.
Quoting the boolean expression so isVisible receives text.
Hiding essential facts behind a toggle.
More than six top-level actions.
troubleshooting: If the toggle does nothing, the target ID does not match the element's id.
If the card fails to post, check the isVisible expression outputs true or false, not empty.
If the ShowCard inputs are missing from the response, their IDs clash with other inputs.
If buttons vanish, reduce primary actions or move some to a ShowCard.
seoTitle: Show and hide parts of an Adaptive Card
seoDescription: Keep cards short with expandable details, a reject button that reveals a reason box, and sections that only appear when the data calls for them.

faqs.question: How do I make part of an Adaptive Card collapsible?
faqs.answer: Give the element an ID with isVisible false and add an Action.ToggleVisibility that targets it.

faqs.question: How do I ask for a reason only when rejecting?
faqs.answer: Use Action.ShowCard on the Reject button with a required text input and its own submit button.

faqs.question: Can a flow hide a section based on data?
faqs.answer: Yes. Set isVisible with an expression that outputs true or false when the card is built.

title: Build a table of rows in an Adaptive Card from an array
shortDescription: Turn a list of items into card rows with the Select action, using ColumnSets or the Table element, and insert the result into the card without a loop.
fullDescription: Cards often need a variable number of rows: open tasks, order lines, overdue items. Building JSON by appending strings in a loop is slow and error-prone. The Select action maps each item to a row object in one step, and the resulting array drops straight into the card body.
problemStatement: A daily digest card should list each overdue task with owner and due date, but the number of tasks changes and string-concatenated JSON keeps breaking on quotes.
whenToUse: Digest cards listing a handful of items
Order or checklist lines in an approval card
Any card with repeating rows
whenNotToUse: More than about 15 rows, where a link to a view is kinder to readers
Cards near the 28 KB Teams size limit
formulaOrCode:
Source
  Get items (SharePoint): Tasks, Filter Query: DueDate lt '@{utcNow()}' and Status ne 'Done', Top Count 15

Option A: ColumnSet rows with Select
  Select
    From: body('Get_items')?['value']
    Map (switch to text mode and paste one object):
    {
      "type": "ColumnSet",
      "separator": true,
      "columns": [
        { "type": "Column", "width": 50, "items": [ { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "@{item()?['Title']}", "wrap": true } ] },
        { "type": "Column", "width": 30, "items": [ { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "@{item()?['AssignedTo/DisplayName']}", "wrap": true } ] },
        { "type": "Column", "width": 20, "items": [ { "type": "TextBlock",
            "text": "@{formatDateTime(item()?['DueDate'],'dd MMM')}", "color": "Attention", "horizontalAlignment": "Right" } ] }
      ]
    }

  Card (Compose, then use its output in the post action)
    {
      "type": "AdaptiveCard", "$schema": "http://adaptivecards.io/schemas/adaptive-card.json", "version": "1.4",
      "body": @{union(
          createArray(
            json('{"type":"TextBlock","text":"Overdue tasks","weight":"Bolder","size":"Medium"}'),
            json('{"type":"ColumnSet","columns":[{"type":"Column","width":50,"items":[{"type":"TextBlock","text":"Task","weight":"Bolder"}]},{"type":"Column","width":30,"items":[{"type":"TextBlock","text":"Owner","weight":"Bolder"}]},{"type":"Column","width":20,"items":[{"type":"TextBlock","text":"Due","weight":"Bolder","horizontalAlignment":"Right"}]}]}')
          ),
          body('Select'))},
      "actions": [ { "type": "Action.OpenUrl", "title": "Open the list", "url": "https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/ops/Lists/Tasks" } ]
    }
  Simpler assembly: put the rows inside a Container
      "body": [
        { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "Overdue tasks (@{length(body('Select'))})", "weight": "Bolder" },
        { "type": "Container", "items": @{body('Select')} }
      ]
  An array output placed directly after "items": produces valid JSON, since the action output is already an array.

Option B: the Table element (version 1.5)
  Select map:
    { "type": "TableRow", "cells": [
        { "type": "TableCell", "items": [ { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "@{item()?['Title']}", "wrap": true } ] },
        { "type": "TableCell", "items": [ { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "@{item()?['AssignedTo/DisplayName']}", "wrap": true } ] },
        { "type": "TableCell", "items": [ { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "@{formatDateTime(item()?['DueDate'],'dd MMM')}" } ] } ] }
  Card body element:
    { "type": "Table", "firstRowAsHeader": false, "showGridLines": true,
      "columns": [ { "width": 5 }, { "width": 3 }, { "width": 2 } ],
      "rows": @{body('Select')} }

Empty result
  Condition: length(body('Get_items')?['value']) is greater than 0. Otherwise skip posting, or post a short
  "Nothing overdue today" message.

Text safety
  Values inside "@{...}" within Select's JSON map are escaped for you, so quotes and line breaks in titles
  do not break the card. Building JSON with concat() does not escape. Avoid it.

Size
  Teams rejects cards above roughly 28 KB. Cap rows with Top Count and add "and 12 more" with a link:
    if(greater(length(body('Get_all')?['value']), 15), concat('and ', string(sub(length(body('Get_all')?['value']), 15)), ' more'), '')
stepByStepInstructions: Get the items and limit the count.
Add a Select action that maps each item to a row object.
Compose the card with the Select output placed in a container's items or a table's rows.
Add a header row and a link to the full list.
Skip or simplify the card when there are no rows.
Check the card size and appearance in Teams.
commonMistakes: Appending JSON strings in an Apply to each.
Posting an empty table.
Unlimited rows that exceed the card size limit.
Using the Table element with card version 1.4.
troubleshooting: If the card is rejected as invalid, run the Compose output through the Adaptive Cards Designer.
If rows show as text, the Select output was wrapped in quotes. Place the expression without surrounding quotes.
If a person or lookup column is blank, use the expanded property path shown in the Get items output.
If the card is too large, reduce Top Count or the number of columns.
seoTitle: Build a table of rows in an Adaptive Card from an array
seoDescription: Turn a list of items into card rows with the Select action, using ColumnSets or the Table element, and insert the result into the card without a loop.
primaryKeyword: Adaptive Card dynamic rows Power Automate

faqs.question: How do I repeat rows in an Adaptive Card from Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Use a Select action to map each item to a ColumnSet or TableRow object and place its output array in the card.

faqs.question: Does Teams support tables in Adaptive Cards?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Table element is available with version 1.5. ColumnSets work in earlier versions.

faqs.question: How big can a Teams Adaptive Card be?
faqs.answer: About 28 KB. Limit the number of rows and link to the full list.

title: Post to a Teams channel from any system with a Workflows webhook
shortDescription: Replace retired Office 365 connector webhooks with a flow that receives an HTTP request and posts a message or card to a channel.
fullDescription: Incoming webhooks built on Office 365 connectors in Teams are being retired. The replacement is a flow using the trigger 'When a Teams webhook request is received'. It gives a URL that monitoring tools, scripts and pipelines can post to, and the flow decides how to format and where to post.
problemStatement: A monitoring tool posts alerts to a Teams channel through an old incoming webhook URL, and Teams shows a notice that the connector will stop working.
whenToUse: Alerts from monitoring, build or deployment tools
Scripts that need to notify a channel
Migrating existing incoming webhook integrations
whenNotToUse: Posting confidential data through an unauthenticated URL
High-volume event streams, which will hit Teams and flow limits
formulaOrCode:
Create it from Teams (quickest)
  Channel > ... > Workflows > "Post to a channel when a webhook request is received" > name it > pick team and
  channel > Add workflow > copy the URL.

Or build it in Power Automate
  Trigger: Microsoft Teams > When a Teams webhook request is received
    Who can trigger the flow: Anyone | Any user in my tenant | Specific users in my tenant
  Action: Apply to each  triggerBody()?['attachments']
            Post card in a chat or channel
              Post as: Flow bot     Post in: Channel     Team / Channel: target
              Adaptive Card: items('Apply_to_each')?['content']

Payload the default template expects (Adaptive Card wrapped as an attachment)
  POST <webhook url>
  Content-Type: application/json
  {
    "type": "message",
    "attachments": [
      {
        "contentType": "application/vnd.microsoft.card.adaptive",
        "content": {
          "type": "AdaptiveCard", "$schema": "http://adaptivecards.io/schemas/adaptive-card.json", "version": "1.4",
          "body": [
            { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "Deployment finished", "weight": "Bolder", "size": "Medium" },
            { "type": "FactSet", "facts": [
              { "title": "Solution", "value": "RequestHub 1.5.0.0" },
              { "title": "Environment", "value": "Production" },
              { "title": "Result", "value": "Succeeded" } ] }
          ],
          "actions": [ { "type": "Action.OpenUrl", "title": "View run", "url": "https://dev.azure.com/contoso/_build/results?buildId=123" } ]
        }
      }
    ]
  }

Send it
  PowerShell:
    $body = Get-Content .\card.json -Raw
    Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri $env:TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
  curl:
    curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @card.json "$TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL"
  Response: 202 Accepted. The post appears a few seconds later.

Accept a simple payload instead (friendlier for scripts)
  Sender posts:  { "title": "Disk space low", "text": "Server APP01 at 92%", "severity": "warning", "url": "https://..." }
  In the flow, build the card yourself:
    "text": "@{triggerBody()?['title']}"
    "color": "@{if(equals(triggerBody()?['severity'],'error'),'Attention',if(equals(triggerBody()?['severity'],'warning'),'Warning','Good'))}"
  Old MessageCard payloads ("@type": "MessageCard") are not rendered by the new trigger. Convert them to
  Adaptive Cards or map their title and text fields in the flow.

Security
  The URL contains a signature (sig=). Anyone holding it can post when the trigger is set to Anyone.
  Keep it in a secret store. Rotate by recreating the flow or re-saving the trigger to regenerate the URL.
  Add a shared secret check: sender includes a header or field, flow Condition compares it with an environment
  variable and Terminates when it does not match.
  For tenant-only callers choose "Any user in my tenant", which requires an Entra token on the request.

Limits and behaviour
  Posts appear as the Flow bot (Workflows), with the flow owner's name shown.
  Private channels: the Flow bot cannot post. Use Post as: User, or a shared channel alternative.
  Teams throttles rapid posting to one channel. Batch alerts or add a digest.
  The flow belongs to its creator: add co-owners, or put it in a solution with a service account as owner.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the webhook workflow from the channel's Workflows menu or build it in Power Automate.
Copy the generated URL into the sending system's secret store.
Send a test Adaptive Card payload and confirm it appears.
Reshape incoming data in the flow if senders cannot produce card JSON.
Add a shared secret check or restrict who can trigger it.
Add co-owners or move the flow into a solution with a service owner.
commonMistakes: Sending old MessageCard JSON and getting an empty post.
Leaving the URL in a script committed to source control.
One personal owner on a flow that production alerting depends on.
Flooding a channel with one post per event.
troubleshooting: If the request returns 400, the body is not valid JSON or lacks the attachments array the flow expects.
If nothing appears but the run succeeded, the card content is invalid. Test it in the designer.
If posting fails in a private channel, change Post as to User.
If the URL stops working, the flow was turned off or deleted. Check its run history and owner.
seoTitle: Post to a Teams channel from any system with a Workflows webhook
seoDescription: Replace retired Office 365 connector webhooks with a flow that receives an HTTP request and posts a message or card to a channel.
primaryKeyword: Teams Workflows webhook replace Office 365 connector

faqs.question: What replaces Teams incoming webhooks?
faqs.answer: A Workflows flow with the trigger When a Teams webhook request is received, which provides a URL to post to.

faqs.question: Does the new webhook accept the old MessageCard format?
faqs.answer: No. Send an Adaptive Card in an attachments array, or have the flow build the card from simple fields.

faqs.question: Is the webhook URL secure?
faqs.answer: It is secret but unauthenticated when set to Anyone. Store it safely and add a shared secret check or tenant restriction.

title: Start a flow when a keyword is mentioned in a Teams channel
shortDescription: Watch channels for words such as urgent or outage, fetch the full message and act on it by creating a ticket or alerting an on-call group.
fullDescription: The Teams connector can start a flow when a message containing chosen keywords is posted in a channel or chat. The trigger returns identifiers and a link, so the flow fetches the message details, filters out noise and then logs or routes it. It suits lightweight triage where people already report problems in a channel.
problemStatement: People post 'the portal is down' in a general channel. Nobody on the support team sees it for an hour, because it was never raised as a ticket.
whenToUse: Turning channel chatter into tracked items
Alerting an on-call group on specific words
Simple triage without a bot
whenNotToUse: Monitoring private conversations without telling the people in them
Keywords so common that the flow fires constantly
formulaOrCode:
Trigger
  Microsoft Teams > When keywords are mentioned
    Message type: Channel            (or Group chat)
    Keywords to search for: outage, urgent, "portal down"        comma-separated. Quotes for phrases.
    Team: IT Support        Channel: General (add more with Add new item)
  Polls about every few minutes. Matches whole words, not case-sensitive.

Outputs
  triggerOutputs()?['body/messageId'], ['body/teamId'], ['body/channelId'], ['body/messageLink'], ['body/conversationId']

Get the text and author
  Microsoft Teams > Get message details
    Message: messageId        Message type: Channel        Team / Channel: from the trigger
  body('Get_message_details')?['body/content']               HTML of the message
  body('Get_message_details')?['from/user/displayName']      author
  body('Get_message_details')?['from/user/id']               Entra object ID
  body('Get_message_details')?['createdDateTime']

Skip noise (Condition, all must be true)
  Author is a person, not the Flow bot:    not(empty(body('Get_message_details')?['from/user/id']))
  Not a reply inside a thread you already handled (optional): empty(body('Get_message_details')?['replyToId'])
  Not containing your own marker text:     not(contains(body('Get_message_details')?['body/content'], 'Logged as'))

Plain text from the HTML
  Content Conversion > Html to text: body('Get_message_details')?['body/content']

Act
  SharePoint > Create item: Tickets
    Title: @{take(body('Html_to_text'), 120)}
    Details: full text        ReportedBy: author email from Office 365 Users > Get user profile (V2) with the object ID
    Source: Teams        Link: triggerOutputs()?['body/messageLink']
    Priority: if(contains(toLower(body('Html_to_text')), 'outage'), 'High', 'Normal')

  Reply in the thread so the poster sees it was picked up
    Microsoft Teams > Reply with a message in a channel
      Post as: Flow bot        Team / Channel: from trigger        Message: messageId
      Reply: Logged as ticket #@{outputs('Create_item')?['body/ID']}. The support team has been notified.

  Alert on-call for high priority
    Post message in a chat or channel > Chat with Flow bot > on-call user, with the message link.

Prevent duplicates
  The same message can match more than once if edited. Before creating, Get items with Filter Query
  TeamsMessageId eq '<messageId>' and Top Count 1, and stop when found. Store messageId on the ticket.

Alternatives
  When a new channel message is added: fires on every message. Filter with your own conditions for more
  complex matching (regular wording, several channels).
  When I am mentioned / When someone reacts to a message: other human-driven triggers.
  A reaction-based approach is often less noisy: act only when a triager adds a specific emoji.
