seoTitle: Validate a Power Apps form with IsMatch: patterns and error labels
seoDescription: Check emails, codes, whole numbers and phone numbers in a Power Apps form with IsMatch, show a message under each input, and enable Submit only when every value passes.
secondaryKeywords: Power Apps disable submit button until valid

faqs.question: Do I need ^ and $ in an IsMatch pattern?
faqs.answer: No. In Power Apps, IsMatch uses MatchOptions.Complete by default, so the pattern already has to match the whole text. Match and MatchAll are different: they look for the pattern anywhere.

faqs.question: Is Match.Email enough to validate an email address?
faqs.answer: It checks for an @ and a domain with a dot, which catches most typing mistakes. It can't tell whether the mailbox exists. To accept only your own domain, use a pattern such as [A-Za-z0-9._%+\-]+@contoso\.com with MatchOptions.IgnoreCase.

faqs.question: Can the IsMatch pattern come from a variable or a SharePoint list?
faqs.answer: No. The pattern and the options must be constants written in the formula. If different records need different formats, use Switch over a few fixed IsMatch calls.

faqs.question: Why use [0-9] instead of \d?
faqs.answer: In the current Power Fx rules, \d also matches digits from other writing systems. [0-9] matches only 0 to 9 in every Power Fx host, which is usually what a code or quantity needs.

title: Extract values from text with Match and MatchAll
shortDescription: Pull a request number, a name and email, or every ID mentioned in a notes field out of free text, with named submatches and a check for no match.
fullDescription: Match returns the first place a pattern fits as a record, and MatchAll returns every place as a table. Named submatches turn the parts you care about into columns, so a subject line, a sender line or a notes field becomes values the app can use.
problemStatement: Useful values arrive buried in text: a request number in an email subject, a name and address in one line, several IDs in a notes field. Left, Mid and Find break as soon as the text shifts by one character.
whenToUse: Text that follows a recognisable shape, such as REQ-00042, an email address or an amount
Reading several parts of one line at once, such as a name and an email
Finding every occurrence of something in a longer text
whenNotToUse: Splitting text on a fixed separator such as a comma. Split is simpler and faster
Searching a large data source. Match and MatchAll aren't delegated, so use them on text already in the app
Parsing JSON. Use ParseJSON instead
stepByStepInstructions: Collect three or four real examples of the text, including one that should not match.
Write the pattern in the Power Fx regex tester with Match or MatchAll selected, and paste the examples as sample text.
Name each part you want with (?<name>...), and check the named submatches the tester shows for each example.
Copy the formula into the app. Wrap a Match in With so it runs once, and check IsBlank before reading a column.
For MatchAll, check IsEmpty, or let an empty gallery show the empty state.
Convert what you read with Value, DateValue or Lower before you save it.
commonMistakes: Reading m.id without checking IsBlank(m) first, which returns blank silently when the text has no match.
Testing MatchAll with IsBlank. It returns an empty table, not blank, so use IsEmpty.
Expecting a case-insensitive match. Add MatchOptions.IgnoreCase as the third argument if req-00042 should match.
Building the pattern from a variable or a column. The pattern must be a constant in the formula.
Naming a submatch FullMatch or StartMatch, which clashes with the columns Match already returns.
Leaving a dot unescaped in a pattern for an amount or a domain, so it matches any character.
troubleshooting: If Match returns blank for text that looks right, paste that exact text into the regex tester. A non-breaking space or a different dash is the usual cause.
If a named submatch column is missing, check that the name starts with a letter and appears as (?<name>...) in the pattern.
If MatchAll returns overlapping or too many results, make the pattern more specific, for example by adding a word boundary \b at each end.
If Power Apps reports that the pattern isn't valid, check the stricter Power Fx 1.0 rules in the regex tester's warnings, such as an unescaped hyphen in [ ].

relatedLinks.label: Test the request number pattern in the regex tester

seoTitle: Extract values from text in Power Apps with Match and MatchAll
seoDescription: Pull a request number, a name and email, or every ID in a notes field out of text in Power Apps with Match, MatchAll and named submatches, and handle text with no match.
secondaryKeywords: get number from text Power Apps

faqs.question: What is the difference between Match and MatchAll?
faqs.answer: Match returns the first match as a record, or blank when there is none. MatchAll returns every match as a table, which is empty when there are none.

faqs.question: How do I read a named submatch?
faqs.answer: Name the part with (?<name>...) in the pattern, then read it as a column: Match(txtSubject.Text, "\[(?<id>REQ-[0-9]{5})\]").id. Check the Match isn't blank first.

faqs.question: Should I use Match or Split?
faqs.answer: Use Split when the text is cut on a fixed separator, such as a comma. Use Match when you need to find a value by its shape somewhere in the text.
